content: The Cadet Nurse Program was overseen by the United States Public Health Service (PHS). Following the United States' entry into World War II, it became evident that the nation would soon face a severe shortage of nurses. As the war progressed, the demand for nurses increased significantly. To address this, it was necessary to train a large number of nursing students rapidly. Consequently, the instructional staff and facilities of existing civilian nursing schools needed to be bolstered. An emergency measure was deemed faster and more cost-effective than reestablishing the Army School of Nursing or constructing similar military hospital-based schools. Additionally, nursing students could undergo accelerated training and contribute their services while still in training. This approach allowed more graduate nurses to be deployed for military service overseas. These plans ensured that both civilian and military communities received substitute nursing care from student nurses on the home front. The plans were formalized when Representative Frances P. Bolton of Ohio introduced a bill on March 29, 1943. The bill proposed the establishment of a special government program to facilitate the training of nurses. It also allocated specific funds to participating accredited nursing schools, aiming to involve as many schools as possible in the Cadet Nurse Program. The Nurse Training Act, also known as the Bolton Act, passed Congress unanimously. President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the bill into law on June 15, 1943, and it became effective as Public Law 74 on July 1, 1943. The Cadet Nurse Corps, initially referred to as the Victory Nurse Corps, was administered by the United States Public Health Service (PHS). Dr. Thomas Parran, the Surgeon General, appointed Lucile Petry, a registered nurse (RN), as the Director of the Cadet Nurse Corps. Nursing schools across the country were informed about the new Corps and invited to participate. Schools wishing to join the program had to meet minimal requirements. They needed to be accredited and affiliated with a hospital approved by the American College of Surgeons. While the staff and facilities had to be adequate, they were not required to meet superior standards. Schools with substandard conditions were not excluded but were instead provided with funds from the Corps to improve their training capabilities. By the time the Cadet Nurse Program concluded, 1,125 out of the nation's 1,300 nursing schools had participated in the initiative.
